This document alone does not provide an authorisation for a pharmacist to prescribe.' (p.1)
protocol.supervision_model: Approved pharmacist prescribing (document's own terminology): pharmacists must be 'approved by the Department of Health to participate in the Enhanced Access Community Pharmacy Pilot (EACPP)' and 'authorised to prescribe under the Medicines and Poisons Regulations 2016 (WA)'; 'Pharmacists must exercise professional discretion and judgement consistent with their qualifications and legislative authority. This guideline does not override the responsibility of the pharmacist to undertake clinical assessments and to make decisions appropriate to the circumstances of the individual and the relevant standards of care, in consultation with the patient and/or their parent/caregiver.' (p.1)
protocol.scope_summary: EACPP clinical practice guideline for hormonal contraception in patients assigned female at birth aged 16 years or over. The service allows prescription of 4 types of hormonal contraception: combined oral contraceptive pill (COC), progestogen-only pill (POP), depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) injection (including administration of the injection), and the combined hormonal contraceptive vaginal ring (p.3). Flow (p.2): meet service and professional obligations -> patient history and assessment (sexual and social history; examination: BMI, blood pressure measurement) -> contraceptive and sexual health plan (select appropriate contraceptive option) -> provide contraception and concurrently refer -> confirm contraception plan is appropriate (contraindications, precautions, interactions; pregnancy and lactation; UKMEC) -> communicate agreed contraceptive plan -> clinical review. 'Refer when' list (p.3) defines referral triggers; a 'Provide contraception and concurrently refer' list (p.4) defines concurrent referral. No product-level doses, strengths or frequencies are printed anywhere in the 18 pages - product detail must come from the Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health (Contraception).

inclusion.text: Service restricted to patients assigned female at birth aged 16 years or over.

This clinical practice guideline may only be used by pharmacists who have been approved by the Department of Health to participate in the Enhanced Access Community Pharmacy Pilot (EACPP) and are authorised to prescribe under the Medicines and Poisons Regulations 2016 (WA). This document alone does not provide an authorisation for a pharmacist to prescribe.
Initial patient eligibility and suitability for management within the scope of the service
Patient informed consent (including consent for communication with other health practitioners if relevant)

Patients are required to have a pharmacist consultation, including blood pressure measurement and BMI calculation, before a hormonal contraceptive method may be prescribed, regardless of whether the patient is currently using the type of contraception requested.

Pharmacists must ensure that they are prescribing medicines according to the specified sections of the current online version of the Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health (Contraception).

exclusion.text: the patient is aged below 16 years (does not preclude a patient from accessing usual pharmacy care)

the patient requests or requires a method of contraception that is not available in the Hormonal Contraception Service e.g. long-acting reversible contraception (LARCs), combined oral contraceptives containing ≥ 50 micrograms ethinylestradiol, or preparations containing mestranol
the patient has unexplained vaginal bleeding, severe or painful menstrual bleeding, irregular periods, amenorrhea, or pain/discomfort with sexual intercourse
the patient may be pregnant (refer to Exclude pregnancy)

the patient has signs and symptoms of PMOS (polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, previously referred to as polycystic ovarian syndrome - PCOS) that have not been assessed by an appropriate healthcare provider
the patient has undiagnosed hypertension, is hypertensive, or has poorly managed hypertension
the preferred contraceptive type is contraindicated or not appropriate (UKMEC 3 or 4).
COCs containing 50 micrograms or more ethinylestradiol, or preparations containing mestranol, are NOT permitted for use in the Hormonal Contraception Service.
A hormonal contraception that is classified as UKMEC category of 3 or 4 for a patient cannot be prescribed as part of the Hormonal Contraception Service.

exclusion_exceptions.text: Ineligibility for treatment as part of a prescribing service does not preclude a patient from accessing services provided as part of usual pharmacy care.

Where the individual is assessed as being a 'mature minor', the additional consent of the minor's parent or guardian is not required before contraceptive advice and treatment can be given (however, it is considered good practice for the parent/caregiver to be involved in decision making around health care).
Parental consent is required where the minor is assessed as not being a 'mature minor' (i.e. not being competent to consent to treatment), except in the case of an emergency.

diagnosis_pathways.name: Hormonal contraception - guideline overview pathway (page 2 flow, elaborated pages 4-13)

steps.description: Meet service and professional obligations: initial patient eligibility and suitability for management within the scope of the service; patient informed consent (including consent for communication with other health practitioners if relevant). Service restricted to patients assigned female at birth aged 16 years or over. 'Ineligibility for treatment as part of a prescribing service does not preclude a patient from accessing services provided as part of usual pharmacy care.'

gates.criterion: Initial patient eligibility and suitability for management within the scope of the service (Refer when: the patient is aged below 16 years)
Patient informed consent (including consent for communication with other health practitioners if relevant)

steps.description: Patient history and assessment - initial consultation: an individualised assessment of contraceptive and sexual health needs, and suitability for hormonal contraception and management within the service should consider: patient history including sexual history; discussion of all available contraceptive options (including options not available in the service that may be suitable); assessment of medical eligibility and contraindications; BP measurement and BMI; risk assessment for STIs. Selection of an appropriate hormonal method and formulation should consider factors that could affect contraceptive effectiveness (including product efficacy); how long the patient thinks they will be using contraception (e.g. < 1 year, < 3 years, > 3 years); non-contraceptive benefits; common side effects and risk of adverse effects; health risks and individualised advice. Comprehensive counselling may include the use of tailored regimens, avoiding contraceptive failure, including instructions on missed pills or DMPA injections. Detailed patient history (p.8 'Patient history'): age; gender assigned at birth and fertility status (for transgender and non-binary patients); plans to become pregnant, current pregnancy status (and how this has been determined); recent pregnancies and lactation status; underlying medical conditions including mental health conditions, which may be a contraindication to hormonal contraception e.g. migraine with aura, liver disease, or impact on contraceptive effectiveness and choice; previous use and experiences with contraception; current and recently ceased treatments (including prescribed medicines, vitamins, herbs, other supplements, and over-the-counter medicines); drug allergies/adverse reactions; prior use of contraceptives, tolerability and adverse effects including mood-related symptoms; smoking status; BMI; other factors such as usual menstrual cycle, heavy periods, period pain or changes in menstrual cycle, irregular or post-coital bleeding, symptoms that may suggest endometriosis (e.g. pelvic pain, severe pain with menstruation and/or sexual intercourse), symptoms that may suggest PMOS (e.g. oligomenorrhea, hirsutism, acne, weight gain); signs or symptoms of menopause or perimenopause; last STI screen and Cervical Screening Test (CST); presence of genitourinary symptoms that may suggest an STI (changes in vaginal or urethral discharge; vulval, genital skin problems or symptoms; lower abdominal pain; dysuria); Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination status. Sexual (and social) history: start by asking open questions about the patient's social background; more specific questions on risk behaviours, followed by questions around sexual practices if required; current relationship status; number of recent partners and their gender; risky behaviours including illicit and/or intravenous drug use, alcohol use; potential for reproductive coercion, sexual and domestic abuse; previous STIs and risk factors for STIs (including STI history of current and/or recent partner if applicable).

gates.criterion: Refer when: the patient has unexplained vaginal bleeding, severe or painful menstrual bleeding, irregular periods, amenorrhea, or pain/discomfort with sexual intercourse
Refer when: the patient has signs and symptoms of PMOS that have not been assessed by an appropriate healthcare provider
Refer when: the patient requests or requires a method of contraception that is not available in the Hormonal Contraception Service
Refer when: the patient may be pregnant

steps.description: Examination: 'The pharmacist should measure the patient's height and weight, and calculate BMI as part of the consultation, as self-reported height and weight may be inaccurate. The pharmacist should measure BP to determine the patient's suitability for their preferred contraceptive type, and to monitor potential impacts of contraception, including hypertension: BP should be measured in accordance with the National Heart Foundation of Australia [and] Guideline for the diagnosis and management of hypertension in adults; a single elevated BP reading is not enough to classify a patient as hypertensive, and a second BP reading should be taken at the end of the consultation.' (p.9). Note (p.9): a patient can be reasonably assumed not to be pregnant only if the Exclude pregnancy criteria in PW-1-S4 are met and they 'have a negative urine pregnancy test' (reference numbers 4, 12 / 17, 18 attach ambiguously across the two columns - see open question).

gates.criterion: Refer when: the patient has undiagnosed hypertension, is hypertensive, or has poorly managed hypertension
Provide contraception and concurrently refer: patient has a body mass index (BMI) > 35 kg/m2

steps.description: Exclude pregnancy: 'Pregnancy should be reasonably excluded before commencing any hormonal contraception.' A patient can be reasonably assumed not to be pregnant if: there are no symptoms or signs of pregnancy AND any of the following criteria are met: they have not had intercourse since the start of the last normal (natural) menstrual period, or since childbirth, abortion, or miscarriage; they have been correctly and consistently using a reliable method of contraception (barrier methods can be assumed to be reliable if used correctly in this context); they are within the first 5 days of the onset of a normal (natural) menstrual period or within the first 5 days after abortion or miscarriage; they are less than 21 days postpartum; they have not had intercourse for > 21 days [and have a negative urine pregnancy test]. 'If there is any doubt regarding whether the patient may be pregnant, even if a negative urine test is returned, hormonal contraception should NOT be prescribed and the patient referred to an appropriate healthcare provider.'

gates.criterion: There are no symptoms or signs of pregnancy AND any one of the listed pregnancy-exclusion criteria is met
If there is any doubt regarding whether the patient may be pregnant, even if a negative urine test is returned - hormonal contraception should NOT be prescribed

steps.description: Contraceptive and sexual health plan - select the most appropriate hormonal contraceptive option (flow step 'Select appropriate contraceptive option', p.2; elaborated pp.10-11): the 4 types available in the Hormonal Contraception Service are the combined oral contraceptive pill, the combined hormonal contraceptive vaginal ring, the progestogen-only contraceptive pill, and depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) injection (including administration of the injection). The choice of hormonal contraception will depend on the patient's history; the patient's preference (cost short and long term; ease of use; management of other conditions including medication history; potential side effects and potential benefits); and contraceptive efficacy (when used correctly, the hormonal methods available in the Hormonal Contraception Service have similar failure rates, but consistency of user adherence is variable and may impact on effectiveness). 'Before prescribing hormonal contraception, pharmacists should discuss the use of LARCs with women seeking contraception, as per the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RANZCOG) recommendations.' COC choice: 'The COC with the lowest effective dose of estrogen and progestogen that is well tolerated and able to provide acceptable menstrual cycle control for the patient should be chosen as first-line'; other guiding principles are safety profile, affordability, and additional non-contraceptive benefits if desired; 'COCs containing 50 micrograms or more ethinylestradiol, or preparations containing mestranol, are NOT permitted for use in the Hormonal Contraception Service'. POP: 'For patients who have a contraindication to estrogen in COC pills or prefer estrogen-free contraception, POPs can be considered'; 'Drospirenone provides more consistent suppression of ovulation than levonorgestrel or norethisterone, and may provide better bleeding control'. DMPA: 'DMPA may be the contraceptive of choice for individuals with contraindications to estrogen, those taking drugs that induce the CYP3A4 liver enzyme ... if a discreet method of contraception is preferred or less user input required'; 'DMPA is not a first-line option for people with higher risk of VTE, as well as adolescents or perimenopausal people because of the theoretical propensity to cause bone mineral density (BMD) loss and/or limit peak BMD'; 'People should be informed that there can be a delay of up to one year in the return of fertility after discontinuation of DPMA'. 'Patients that require assistance with insertion of a vaginal ring should be referred to an appropriate healthcare provider.'

gates.criterion: Refer when: the patient requests or requires a method of contraception that is not available in the Hormonal Contraception Service (e.g. LARCs, combined oral contraceptives containing ≥ 50 micrograms ethinylestradiol, or preparations containing mestranol)
Refer when: the preferred contraceptive type is contraindicated or not appropriate (UKMEC 3 or 4)
COCs containing 50 micrograms or more ethinylestradiol, or preparations containing mestranol, are NOT permitted for use in the Hormonal Contraception Service
Patients that require assistance with insertion of a vaginal ring should be referred to an appropriate healthcare provider

steps.description: Provide contraception and concurrently refer - 'Provide initial treatment and concurrently refer to an appropriate healthcare provider (including sexual health service or emergency services, if required) in the following situations: patient has been, or suspected to have been, subject to reproductive coercion, sexual abuse or sexual violence (refer to Reproductive coercion, sexual and domestic violence and abuse); patient has a body mass index (BMI) > 35 kg/m2; patient has symptoms of or risk factors for sexually transmitted infection (STI) or requests STI screening.' Treatment proceeds while the concurrent referral is made. Reproductive coercion section (p.6): 'If the pharmacist becomes aware of this during the consultation, they should provide appropriate support and assistance, including referral to support options depending on the patient circumstances. Referral options include to the local hospital, sexual health clinic, and/or community-based sexual violence support services.'

gates.criterion: patient has been, or suspected to have been, subject to reproductive coercion, sexual abuse or sexual violence
patient has a body mass index (BMI) > 35 kg/m2
patient has symptoms of or risk factors for sexually transmitted infection (STI) or requests STI screening

steps.description: Confirm contraception plan is appropriate: 'The agreed management plan should be shared with members of the patient's multidisciplinary healthcare team, with the patient's consent.' 'Consult the current editions of the Therapeutic Guidelines, the Australian Medicines Handbook, and the UKMEC to confirm contraceptive management is appropriate, including for: contraindications and precautions; drug interactions; pregnancy and lactation. It is the pharmacist's responsibility to ensure the suitability and accuracy of any resources provided to patients (and parent/caregiver if applicable), and to ensure compliance with all copyright conditions. A hormonal contraception that is classified as UKMEC category of 3 or 4 for a patient cannot be prescribed as part of the Hormonal Contraception Service.' (p.12). Other considerations: Venous Thromboembolism ('There may be a small increased risk of VTE with the use of DMPA. Other progestogen-only contraceptives are not associated with a clinically significant risk of VTE'; 'There is approximately a 3 times increase in the risk of VTE in people using COC, however, this increased risk is still smaller than the risk of VTE during pregnancy and immediately post-partum'; 'The risk is highest in the first year of use ...'; 'COCs containing levonorgestrel or norethisterone have a slightly lower risk of VTE'); Contraception and cancer risks ('Users of COC have a slightly increased relative risk of breast cancer (risk returns to normal 10 years after cessation of the OCP) and cervical cancer (non-causal), however, the risk of endometrial and ovarian cancers is slightly decreased').

gates.criterion: A hormonal contraception classified as UKMEC category 3 or 4 for the patient cannot be prescribed as part of the Hormonal Contraception Service
Confirm for: contraindications and precautions; drug interactions; pregnancy and lactation

steps.description: Communicate agreed contraceptive plan: 'Comprehensive advice and counselling (including supporting written information when required) should be provided to the patient regarding: individual product and medicine use - instructions for commencing; deviation from schedule (e.g. a pill is missed, a DMPA injection is not administered between 10 to 14 weeks post previous dose, or a new vaginal ring is inserted too late or removed before the 3-week interval); how long a secondary method of contraception must be used to avoid unplanned pregnancy; instructions on tailored regimens; advice on when fertility can be expected to return after ceasing the contraceptive; emergency contraceptive options that are available in instances of contraceptive failure (see Emergency contraception, p.6); how to manage adverse effects; when to seek further care and/or treatment - signs of VTE and what to do if it is suspected; the importance of reporting new or worsening mood-related symptoms; before ceasing the contraceptive; review with an appropriate healthcare provider at least every 2 years; when to return for follow-up.' Also general advice and patient information, and communication with other health practitioners (flow, p.2).

gates.criterion: when to seek further care and/or treatment: signs of VTE and what to do if it is suspected

steps.description: Clinical review (flow, p.2: Measure BP; Adverse effects; Continue, change, or stop contraception; Communication with other health practitioners). 'Clinical review with the pharmacist (or the patient's chosen healthcare provider) should occur in line with recommendations in the Therapeutic Guidelines: patients should return for a follow up consultation 3 to 4 months after initiation of a new contraceptive method (i.e. the patient has no recent experience of taking that type of contraception) to screen for adverse effects including hypertension; clinical review, including measurement of the patient's BP and BMI is recommended at 12-monthly intervals for all patients on regular hormonal contraception; for patients continuing therapy, follow-up should be individualised to the patient's clinical presentation, response to treatment, and therapeutic goals. Pharmacists should prescribe a quantity of medicine (including repeats) that aligns with the expected duration of therapy, ensuring sufficient supply until the patient's next review. The total quantity prescribed should not exceed 12 months' supply (including repeats).'

gates.criterion: Follow up consultation 3 to 4 months after initiation of a new contraceptive method to screen for adverse effects including hypertension

treatments.max_quantity: The total quantity prescribed should not exceed 12 months' supply (including repeats).
treatments.quantity_to_supply: The total quantity prescribed should not exceed 12 months' supply (including repeats); quantity aligns with the expected duration of therapy, ensuring sufficient supply until the patient's next review (p.13).
treatments.notes: One of the 4 types of hormonal contraception prescribable under the service (p.3). No product names, strengths, doses, frequencies or durations are printed anywhere in the guideline - product-level detail must come from the Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health (Contraception), specifically the 'Formulations of combined hormonal contraception' table (p.11). Product prohibition verbatim (p.10): 'COCs containing 50 micrograms or more ethinylestradiol, or preparations containing mestranol, are NOT permitted for use in the Hormonal Contraception Service.' First-line statement verbatim (p.11): 'The COC with the lowest effective dose of estrogen and progestogen that is well tolerated and able to provide acceptable menstrual cycle control for the patient should be chosen as first-line.' Other guiding principles (p.11): safety profile, affordability, and additional non-contraceptive benefits if desired; 'Newer progestogens reduce the potential for androgenic, estrogenic, and glucocorticoid effects, but increase the VTE risk'; 'The quadriphasic pill is indicated for heavy menstrual bleeding as well as contraception, but it has complex instructions for managing a missed pill'; 'Triphasic pills are no longer commonly used because of a lack of benefits over other types'; 'COCs with a high estrogen dose (50 micrograms of ethinylestradiol or containing mestranol) are not routinely recommended for contraception because of the unacceptable risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE). These formulations are not permitted for use in the Hormonal Contraception Service.' VTE (p.12): 'There is approximately a 3 times increase in the risk of VTE in people using COC, however, this increased risk is still smaller than the risk of VTE during pregnancy and immediately post-partum'; 'The risk is highest in the first year of use, and still remains higher than for non-users after the first year, however the absolute risk is still very low'; 'COCs containing levonorgestrel or norethisterone have a slightly lower risk of VTE'. Cancer risks (p.12): slightly increased relative risk of breast cancer (risk returns to normal 10 years after cessation of the OCP) and cervical cancer (non-causal), risk of endometrial and ovarian cancers slightly decreased. Pregnancy/lactation caveat (p.12): confirm management including 'pregnancy and lactation' before prescribing; a hormonal contraception classified as UKMEC 3 or 4 cannot be prescribed as part of the service.

treatments.quantity_to_supply: The total quantity prescribed should not exceed 12 months' supply (including repeats) (p.13).

The document does not print the injection route/site, strength, dose or needle - route field is therefore blank; do not infer. No product-level dosing printed. Statements verbatim: 'DMPA may be the contraceptive of choice for individuals with contraindications to estrogen, those taking drugs that induce the CYP3A4 liver enzyme (refer to the Australian Medicines Handbook) if a discreet method of contraception is preferred or less user input required' (p.11); 'DMPA is not a first-line option for people with higher risk of VTE, as well as adolescents or perimenopausal people because of the theoretical propensity to cause bone mineral density (BMD) loss and/or limit peak BMD' (p.11); 'during each annual consultation, pharmacists should assess the user's risk factors for VTE, low BMD, and cardiovascular disease' (p.11); 'people who wish to continue using DMPA should be reviewed by an appropriate healthcare provider every 2 years to assess any changes in benefits and potential risks of use' (p.11); 'People should be informed that there can be a delay of up to one year in the return of fertility after discontinuation of DPMA' (p.11, 'DPMA' as printed); schedule deviation verbatim (p.12): 'a DMPA injection is not administered between 10 to 14 weeks post previous dose'; 'There may be a small increased risk of VTE with the use of DMPA' (p.12). Pregnancy/lactation check required per 'Confirm contraceptive plan is appropriate' (p.12).

Not prescribed as part of the Hormonal Contraception Service; captured because the guideline directs its supply under usual pharmacy care. Verbatim (p.6): 'If emergency contraception (EC) is required, oral EC may be supplied as per usual pharmacy care, refer to the Australian Pharmaceutical Formulary and Handbook (APF): Treatment guidelines for pharmacists (Emergency contraception). Insertion of a copper intrauterine device (IUD) is the most effective form of EC. The patient will require referral to an appropriate medical practitioner or health service for IUD insertion. Contact the Sexual Health Helpline for further information.' No EC product name, strength, dose or timing is printed. Communicate agreed contraceptive plan also requires counselling on 'emergency contraceptive options that are available in instances of contraceptive failure' (p.12).

review_followup.when: 3 to 4 months after initiation of a new contraceptive method
review_followup.what: patients should return for a follow up consultation 3 to 4 months after initiation of a new contraceptive method (i.e. the patient has no recent experience of taking that type of contraception) to screen for adverse effects including hypertension.

review_followup.when: 12-monthly intervals for all patients on regular hormonal contraception
review_followup.what: clinical review, including measurement of the patient's BP and BMI is recommended at 12-monthly intervals for all patients on regular hormonal contraception.
follow-up should be individualised to the patient's clinical presentation, response to treatment, and therapeutic goals.

review_followup.when: Review with an appropriate healthcare provider at least every 2 years
review_followup.what: Communicate agreed contraceptive plan: advice includes when to seek further care and/or treatment, 'review with an appropriate healthcare provider at least every 2 years' and when to return for follow-up.

during each annual consultation, pharmacists should assess the user's risk factors for VTE, low BMD, and cardiovascular disease; people who wish to continue using DMPA should be reviewed by an appropriate healthcare provider every 2 years to assess any changes in benefits and potential risks of use.

review_followup.when: At the age of 50 years and at menopause
review_followup.what: The choice of contraceptive should be reconsidered at the age of 50 years and at menopause. Switching from an oestrogen-containing method or DPMA to an alternative progestogen only or non-hormonal method is advised. Contraception is required for 12 months after the final menstrual period if it occurs after the age of 50; if the final menstrual period occurs before the age of 50, 24 months of contraception is required before cessation. If it is unclear when contraception can be ceased, refer to a medical practitioner.

review_followup.when: At the time of initial consultation (advice on return triggers)
review_followup.what: Communicate agreed contraceptive plan: counselling must cover when to seek further care and/or treatment (signs of VTE and what to do if it is suspected; the importance of reporting new or worsening mood-related symptoms; before ceasing the contraceptive) and when to return for follow-up.

More information is available on the Department of Communities Child Protection website.' (conditional on the pharmacist considering there may be child protection concerns)

open_questions.topic: No product-level doses, strengths, frequencies or durations are printed for any of the four contraceptive methods
open_questions.observed: Across all 18 pages no drug product name, strength, dose, dosing frequency or treatment duration appears for the COC, POP, DMPA injection or vaginal ring; page 10-11 defer to 'the specified sections of the current online version of the Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health (Contraception)' and the 'Formulations of combined hormonal contraception table'.
open_questions.why_unclear: TX-1 to TX-4 therefore have blank strength/dose/frequency fields; nothing can be transcribed without inventing it. Dosing must come from the specified sections of the current online Therapeutic Guidelines.

open_questions.topic: No first-line ranking is printed between the four service methods
open_questions.observed: The four types are listed as a set (p.3). The only first-line statement is internal to COC choice: 'The COC with the lowest effective dose of estrogen and progestogen ... should be chosen as first-line' (p.11). DMPA 'is not a first-line option' for higher VTE risk, adolescents or perimenopausal people (p.11). LARCs must be discussed (p.3) but cannot be prescribed in this service.
open_questions.why_unclear: first_line is set false on all four method rows because the document gives no ranking between them; this reflects the source rather than a judgement that none is first line.

open_questions.topic: No numeric blood pressure threshold is printed for the hypertension referral trigger
open_questions.observed: Refer when (p.3): 'the patient has undiagnosed hypertension, is hypertensive, or has poorly managed hypertension'. Examination (p.9): 'a single elevated BP reading is not enough to classify a patient as hypertensive, and a second BP reading should be taken at the end of the consultation'; BP to be measured 'in accordance with the National Heart Foundation of Australia ... Guideline for the diagnosis and management of hypertension in adults' - no mmHg value is printed in this document.
open_questions.why_unclear: RF-6/EXC-6 must stay qualitative; an automatic numeric check cannot be derived from this document alone.

open_questions.topic: Page 9 two-column extraction interleaves the pregnancy-exclusion bullet with the BP column
open_questions.observed: Text order on page 9 reads: '... they have not had intercourse for > 21 days' / '• BP should be measured in accordance with the National Heart Foundation of Australia' / reference '4, 12' / 'and have a negative urine pregnancy test .' / 'Guideline for the diagnosis and management of hypertension in adults' / '17 If there is any doubt ...' / '... referred to an appropriate healthcare provider.' / '17, 18.'
open_questions.why_unclear: It is not certain from the extraction whether 'and have a negative urine pregnancy test' completes the last pregnancy-exclusion bullet (with refs 4,12) or belongs to the BP column, nor which reference numbers attach to which sentence. PW-1-S4 records both readings ('they have not had intercourse for > 21 days [and have a negative urine pregnancy test]') with confidence 'medium'; PW-1-S3 carries confidence 'unclear' for the same reason.

open_questions.topic: The Refer when list is printed twice with minor wording differences
open_questions.observed: The eight right-hand column items on page 2 ('Guideline overview - Refer when') repeat as the seven-item 'Refer when' section on page 3. Page 2 words the BMI item and STI item under 'Provide contraception and concurrently refer' rather than under 'Refer when', and page 3 adds the UKMEC qualifier '(UKMEC 3 or 4)' and the LARC/≥50 micrograms/mestranol examples.
open_questions.why_unclear: The list was captured once with provenance to page 3 (the dedicated section) and the concurrent items with provenance to page 4; the page 2 duplicates are noted here so the duplication is not lost.

open_questions.topic: PMOS terminology used by the document
open_questions.observed: The guideline writes 'PMOS (polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, previously referred to as polycystic ovarian syndrome - PCOS)' in both the overview and the Refer when list, and uses 'symptoms that may suggest PMOS (e.g. oligomenorrhea, hirsutism, acne, weight gain)' in the history.
open_questions.why_unclear: Transcribed exactly as printed; 'PMOS' is not standard Australian usage (PCOS is) and an engine keying on 'PCOS' would miss it.

open_questions.observed: Referral destinations/criteria are printed on page 3 (Refer when), page 4 (Provide contraception and concurrently refer), page 5 (young people), page 6 (reproductive coercion, IUD insertion, capacity), page 7 (cessation of contraception), page 11 (vaginal ring insertion) and page 13 (Sexual Health Helpline).
open_questions.why_unclear: Spec rule for the referral block: the shared provenance uses the first page (page 3); the range 3-13 is recorded here.

open_questions.topic: No separately worded urgent referral tier
open_questions.observed: The document distinguishes only 'an appropriate healthcare provider (including sexual health service or emergency services, if required)'. No 'urgent', 'immediate', ambulance or emergency-department wording appears.
open_questions.why_unclear: referral.urgent is empty; emergency holds the printed '(including sexual health service or emergency services, if required)' qualifier rather than a distinct emergency list.

open_questions.topic: Eligibility wording vs gender identity section
open_questions.observed: Page 1: 'Service restricted to patients assigned female at birth aged 16 years or over.' Page 7: 'Current gender identity for trans or non-binary people assigned female at birth does not impose any restrictions on methods of contraception that may be used.'
open_questions.why_unclear: Eligibility keys on sex assigned at birth, not gender identity; the interplay (a trans or non-binary person assigned male at birth is outside the printed restriction) is not addressed by the document.

open_questions.observed: Page 11: 'Switching from an oestrogen-containing method or DPMA to an alternative progestogen only or non-hormonal method is advised' and 'a delay of up to one year in the return of fertility after discontinuation of DPMA'.
open_questions.why_unclear: Transcribed as printed ('DPMA'); presumably means DMPA (depot medroxyprogesterone acetate) but the document is not corrected silently.

open_questions.topic: Combinatorics are inferred from the document's own framing
open_questions.observed: 'Service restricted to patients assigned female at birth aged 16 years or over' and 'may only be used by pharmacists who...' imply AND for the inclusion criteria (INC-1 to INC-6); 'Refer the patient ... in the following situations:' introduces the seven refer-when items as alternatives, implying OR (EXC-1 to EXC-7).
open_questions.why_unclear: The document never prints 'all of' or 'any of' explicitly; the all_of/any_of groups are inferred from that wording and recorded here per spec rule 4.

open_questions.topic: No version number or date printed
open_questions.observed: No version, date, document ID or approving officer appears; page 18 shows footer code "62'GUA80510-DEC", 'Produced by Clinical Excellence Division' and '© Department of Health 2026'.
open_questions.why_unclear: instrument_version and effective_date cannot be populated beyond what is printed.

open_questions.topic: Notifiable requirement is conditional and judgement-based
open_questions.observed: Page 6: 'Pharmacists should consider whether there may be child protection concerns relating to a request for contraception and report to the Department of Communities accordingly.' No notifiable disease, AIR or compulsory GP notification is mentioned.
open_questions.why_unclear: notifiable.required is set true solely on this conditional child-protection reporting statement; the trigger is pharmacist judgement, so the condition is recorded verbatim and flagged in hugh_to_confirm.

open_questions.topic: Source and adaptation acknowledged: originally Queensland Health material
open_questions.observed: Page 18: 'This document is based on clinical guidelines/protocols originally developed by Queensland Health for the Queensland Community Pharmacy Pilots. Queensland Health is acknowledged as the source of the original material.'
open_questions.why_unclear: Recorded for provenance of the instrument; no version of the Queensland originals is cited, so the WA document's own version cannot be derived from it.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm each pharmacist's EACPP approval and authorisation to prescribe under the Medicines and Poisons Regulations 2016 (WA), since 'This document alone does not provide an authorisation for a pharmacist to prescribe'.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Eligibility to use the guideline is conditional on departmental approval and authorisation that this document cannot evidence.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm which sections of the current online version of the Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health (Contraception) are the 'specified sections' pharmacists must prescribe according to (page 10) - the guideline does not enumerate them.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: INC-6 makes this a mandatory prescribing condition, but without the section list it cannot be evaluated as a hard check before go-live.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Obtain product-level drug names, strengths, doses, frequencies and quantities for the COC, POP, DMPA injection and vaginal ring from the Therapeutic Guidelines before any dosing rule is encoded - none are printed in this guideline.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: TX-1 to TX-4 have blank strength/dose/frequency fields; a prescribing support module cannot issue supply instructions from class names alone.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm the numeric blood-pressure threshold(s) that make a patient 'undiagnosed hypertensive, hypertensive, or poorly managed hypertensive' for the referral rule (page 3), given page 9 only says a single elevated reading is not enough and a second reading should be taken at the end of the consultation.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: RF-6/EXC-6 cannot be implemented as an automatic check without a printed threshold; the National Heart Foundation guideline reference is external.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm the operational supply rule: total quantity prescribed (including repeats) must not exceed 12 months' supply - including how 'sufficient supply until the patient's next review' interacts with stock, repeats, the 3-4 month follow-up and the 12-monthly review.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Hard cap printed in the guideline but the interaction of duration-of-therapy vs quantity-supplied vs review interval is left to the pharmacist and local supply policy.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm the local process for 'Provide contraception and concurrently refer' (BMI > 35 kg/m2; STI symptoms/risk factors or screening request; reproductive coercion/sexual abuse/sexual violence) - whether the contraceptive is supplied in the same visit while the referral proceeds, and which destinations are used.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: The document requires concurrent treatment and referral but leaves destination and sequencing to the pharmacist; this is a local workflow decision.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm the 'mature minor' assessment process, its documentation requirement ('Assessments of capacity to consent for minors ... must be documented in the patient record'), and the parental-consent rules for 16 and 17 year olds seeking treatment without parental knowledge or consent (pages 5-6).
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Jurisdictionally sensitive WA consent law is applied through pharmacist judgement; the document defers to the WA legal resources it cites and to the pharmacist's determination.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm the child-protection reporting pathway to the Department of Communities and the criteria that trigger it (page 6), plus local policy on recording the decision.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: 'Pharmacists should consider whether there may be child protection concerns' is judgement-based; notifiable.required was set true solely on this conditional statement.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm whether the absence of a first-line ranking between the four methods (and the RANZCOG-mandated LARC discussion, which cannot be fulfilled by prescribing LARCs in this service) should be encoded as sequencing logic, and how the LARC discussion is documented.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: All treatment rows carry first_line false; a treatment-sequencing rule and an LARC-discussion checklist item cannot be derived from this guideline alone.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm the controlled version/date of this clinical practice guideline with the Department of Health (no version or date is printed; only footer code "62'GUA80510-DEC" and © Department of Health 2026).
hugh_to_confirm.reason: A clinical practice guideline used for funded prescribing must be version-controlled and traceable to an approval date.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm the intended reading of the page 9 pregnancy-exclusion bullet 'they have not had intercourse for > 21 days' - whether it continues 'and have a negative urine pregnancy test', and which reference numbers (4, 12 vs 17, 18) attach to it.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Two-column extraction interleaves the text; the ambiguity affects an automatic pregnancy-exclusion rule and is recorded with confidence 'medium'/'unclear'.
